prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that introduces a False Choice, then select the strongest Deliberative pivot.

passage_segments.text: Our legacy database migrations have missed three deadlines this quarter.
Either we freeze all feature development for six months, or the entire platform will collapse by winter.
Management needs to answer for why they hired underqualified contractors last year.

follow_up_question.question: Which response best neutralises the fallacy while keeping the argument in the Deliberative (future) tense?

options.text: The platform won't collapse. You're catastrophising over a minor delay.
options.feedback: Direct contradiction ('nuh-uh') with no forward-looking choice, and it labels the speaker.

options.text: Freezing all features and risking collapse aren't our only options. Let's isolate the highest-risk schema tables this sprint and keep core feature work moving.
options.feedback: Exposes the False Choice and immediately proposes a concrete Deliberative action.

options.text: First we need to understand why the contractors were hired.
options.feedback: Follows the bait in sentence 3 back into forensic blame.

options.text: Then freezing features is the responsible choice.
options.feedback: Accepts the dilemma as framed.

explanation_formal: Sentence 2 is a False Dilemma: it artificially restricts the solution space to two extremes. Sentence 3 drags the stasis backward into forensic blame.
explanation_modern: Sentence 2 traps the listener in a black-and-white False Choice, while sentence 3 plays the Blame Game (past tense) instead of fixing the problem.

prompt_instruction: Diagnose the exchange and choose your reply.

passage_segments.text: Speaker: “Remote work is destroying company culture.”
Challenger: “Our engagement scores went up after we went remote.”
Speaker: “All I'm saying is that some things are harder to do over video.”

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.question: What manoeuvre does the speaker make in the last line?

options.text: Motte-and-Bailey: retreating to a modest claim when the bold one is challenged
options.feedback: Yes. The bold claim gets swapped for a near-truism under fire.
The speaker isn't distorting the challenger's view. They're shrinking their own.
Related topic, but the tell is the retreat to a weaker version of the same claim.
No single word changes meaning. It's two different claims.

steps.label: Locate
steps.question: Which is the bailey, the bold, valuable but hard-to-defend claim?

options.feedback: Right. That's the territory the speaker actually wants.

options.text: “Some things are harder to do over video.”
options.feedback: That's the motte, the easily defended fallback.
That's the challenger's evidence.
There is: the opening line.

options.text: So you admit you were wrong.
options.feedback: Gloating costs you ethos, and they'll simply return to the bailey later.

options.text: Video calls are perfectly fine, actually.
options.feedback: Now you're attacking the motte, which is the defensible part.

options.text: Agreed, some things are harder over video. Is your original claim, that remote work is destroying our culture, still on the table? If so, what would show it?
options.feedback: Grant the motte, then pin the bailey down and ask for its evidence.

options.text: Back in 2019 the office was worse anyway.
options.feedback: A forensic detour that ignores the manoeuvre.

explanation_formal: The motte-and-bailey (Shackel) pairs a desirable but contestable claim (the bailey) with a modest, defensible one (the motte), retreating to the latter when challenged and reoccupying the former when the challenge passes.
explanation_modern: Big claim, pushback, tiny claim, and next week the big claim is back. Concede the tiny claim and make them own or drop the big one.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where the Kafka Trap springs.

passage_segments.text: The culture audit concluded that our team habitually covers up mistakes.
When Lee said he had never hidden an error, the auditor recorded it as “defensiveness consistent with a cover-up culture”.
Two colleagues who agreed with the finding were described as “admirably candid”.
The report goes to the board next week.

follow_up_question.question: What's the strongest response to the audit's method?

options.text: What would we observe if there were no cover-up culture? If both denial and agreement confirm the finding, nothing could ever count against it.
options.feedback: Yes. Expose the unfalsifiability without attacking anyone.

options.text: The auditor is clearly biased against us.
options.feedback: Ad hominem. It also looks exactly like the 'defensiveness' they predicted.
Capitulating to an unfalsifiable claim teaches nothing.

options.text: Lee is the most honest person on the team.
options.feedback: Character testimony doesn't touch the logical trap.

explanation_formal: The Kafka Trap makes the accusation unfalsifiable: denial is reinterpreted as evidence of guilt, so no possible response could disconfirm it.
explanation_modern: Heads I win, tails you lose: deny it and you're defensive, agree and you're candid. Ask what evidence could ever show the claim was false.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where a key word quietly changes meaning.

passage_segments.text: The contract requires the supplier to deliver a “working” prototype by June.
The prototype boots and runs the demo script, so it is working.
Therefore the supplier has met its obligations in full.
That it crashes under any real load is a separate matter for phase two.

options.text: “Working” shifts from “fit for its agreed purpose” to “runs at all”.
options.feedback: Yes. The contract's sense and the supplier's sense are different claims.
Nobody claims it's final.
Dates aren't the issue.

options.text: There's no swap. It boots, so it works.
options.feedback: That's the equivocation talking.

explanation_formal: The argument equivocates on 'working': the contractual sense (fit for purpose) appears in the premise and the minimal sense (operational at all) in the inference.
explanation_modern: Same word, two meanings. The contract meant 'does the job', the supplier means 'switches on'. Pin the definition down before anyone signs off.

prompt_instruction: Your opponent has just said this in a 60-second turn. Diagnose and respond.

passage_segments.text: The four-day week is a disaster. Productivity always falls. Customers hate it. The Iceland trial was rigged.
It costs more than it saves. Staff just take second jobs. And every company that tried it went back within a year.

options.feedback: Yes: many quick, unsupported claims, more than you can answer in your turn.
There's no retreat to a modest claim.
Nothing makes your denial count as evidence.
The claims aren't circular, just numerous and unsupported.

options.text: Answer every claim briefly, in order.
options.feedback: You'll run out of time and look like you're losing.

options.text: Name the pattern, pick the claim their case rests on, and refute that one thoroughly.
options.feedback: Right. Depth beats breadth, and naming it makes the audience see the volume as weakness.

options.text: Gallop back with seven claims of your own.
options.feedback: Now it's two firehoses and no argument.

options.text: Refuse to respond until they slow down.
options.feedback: Concedes the floor.

options.text: You've made seven claims in a minute. Rather than skim all seven, let's test the one your case rests on: that it costs more than it saves.
options.feedback: Names the tactic calmly and chooses the load-bearing claim.

options.text: Literally none of that is true.
options.feedback: Your own overclaim, and just as unsupported.

options.text: The Iceland trial wasn't rigged, productivity didn't fall, customers don't hate it…
options.feedback: You've accepted their battlefield.

options.text: You clearly haven't read any research.
options.feedback: Ad hominem. You also can't know it.

explanation_formal: The Gish Gallop exploits the asymmetry between asserting and refuting. The counter is to make that asymmetry explicit and concentrate refutation on the argument's load-bearing claim.
explanation_modern: A claim takes five seconds to make and five minutes to debunk. Say so, then take apart the one claim the whole case leans on.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that builds the straw man.

passage_segments.text: My colleague proposes that staff may work from home one day a week.
So apparently we're meant to abandon the office entirely and let everyone set their own hours.
That would make collaboration impossible.
I'd urge us to keep things as they are.

follow_up_question.question: Choose the best reply from the colleague.

options.text: I proposed one day a week, not abandoning the office. Do you have evidence that one remote day harms collaboration?
options.feedback: Restates the real position briefly and puts the burden back where it belongs.

options.text: That's a ridiculous exaggeration and you know it.
options.feedback: True, but heat without direction.

options.text: Actually, abandoning the office might be good.
options.feedback: Now you're defending the straw man.
Concedes their frame and alienates the room.

explanation_formal: Sentence 1 states the position accurately. Sentence 2 replaces it with an extreme distortion, which sentences 3–4 then refute.
explanation_modern: One day a week becomes 'abandon the office'. Don't defend the scarecrow. Restate what you actually said.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where the speaker picks the weakest opponent to argue against.

passage_segments.text: Opponents of the bypass have raised a range of objections over the past year.
The county ecologist's report warns that it would cut through the last ancient woodland in the district.
But let's be honest about the opposition: one protester last week claimed the road would “poison every well in the valley”.
Objections of that quality hardly deserve a hearing.

follow_up_question.question: Why is this a weak man rather than a straw man?

options.text: The protester really said it. The fault is choosing the weakest real objection and ignoring the strongest.
options.feedback: Exactly. The quote is accurate, but the selection is the distortion.
Probably not, and that isn't the point.

options.text: Because it attacks the ecologist personally.
options.feedback: The ecologist is ignored, not attacked.
A straw man invents a position. A weak man cherry-picks a real one.

explanation_formal: The weak man (Talisse & Aikin) refutes an actual but unrepresentative advocate. The speaker passes over the strongest objection (s2) to dismiss the class through its weakest member (s3–s4).
explanation_modern: The quote is real. The trick is the cherry-pick: answer the silliest critic and act as if the ecologist's report never existed.

prompt_instruction: Click the personal attack.

passage_segments.text: Dr Okafor's study found the drug reduced hospital admissions by 12%.
But Dr Okafor has been divorced twice and can't keep her own life in order.
So I wouldn't put much stock in her numbers.
The trial involved 4,000 patients across nine hospitals.

follow_up_question.question: Which of these is a legitimate challenge rather than an ad hominem?

options.text: Was the trial pre-registered, and were admissions measured the same way in both arms?
options.feedback: Yes. It goes after the method, which is where the numbers come from.
Character, not evidence.
Prestige by association. It doesn't touch the data.
Insinuated motive with no evidence of a conflict.

explanation_formal: Sentence 2 is an abusive ad hominem: personal life has no bearing on the trial data. A documented conflict of interest would be a reason to scrutinise the method more closely, not to dismiss the result.
explanation_modern: Her divorces don't change the admission numbers. If you doubt the study, question the study.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that treats absence of evidence as proof.

passage_segments.text: We've run the new caching layer in staging for a week.
Nobody has reported a single bug.
So it's proven bug-free and ready for production.
Staging traffic is about 2% of production volume.

follow_up_question.question: Which sentence most undermines the conclusion?

options.text: Sentence 4: staging sees about 2% of production traffic.
options.feedback: Yes. With so little traffic, few bugs would have had the chance to show up.
Relevant, but the traffic volume matters more than the duration.
That's the evidence the argument rests on.
Sentence 4 does real damage.

explanation_formal: From 'no bugs reported' to 'proven bug-free' is an argument from ignorance, compounded by overclaiming ('proven') and weakened by the low test exposure in sentence 4.
explanation_modern: Nobody saw a bug is not the same as there being no bugs, especially when hardly anyone was looking.

prompt_instruction: Diagnose the reasoning, then choose what would fix it.

passage_segments.text: We can trust the quarterly forecast because it comes from the forecasting team.
And the forecasting team is trustworthy because their forecasts are reliable.

options.text: It's circular: the forecasts are trusted because of the team, and the team because of the forecasts.
options.feedback: Yes, petitio principii. The conclusion props up its own premise.
It praises the team rather than attacking anyone, and it's still circular.
No options are being restricted.

options.text: Nothing. It's a reasonable appeal to expertise.
options.feedback: An appeal to expertise needs independent grounds for the expertise.

options.text: An independent track record: how past forecasts compared with actual results.
options.feedback: Right. External evidence gives the argument a foundation outside itself.
Still authority vouching for itself.
Confidence isn't evidence.

options.text: Asking the team whether they're reliable.
options.feedback: That's the circle again.

explanation_formal: Petitio principii: the reliability of the forecasts is both what's being proved and what's being assumed. Only independent evidence (backing) can ground the warrant.
explanation_modern: 'Trust them because they're trustworthy' goes round in a circle. You need outside evidence: check last year's forecasts against what actually happened.

prompt_instruction: Click the red herring.

passage_segments.text: The question tonight is whether the school day should start at 9 a.m. instead of 8:15.
Research on teenage sleep suggests later starts improve attendance and attention.
Mr Hale argues against the change.
He points out that teachers already work long hours and deserve a pay rise.
And who could disagree with that?

explanation_formal: Sentence 4 introduces a sympathetic but distinct issue (teacher pay) and so proves a conclusion other than the one in question. Sentence 5 then invites assent to the substituted issue.
explanation_modern: The debate is about start times. Teacher pay may matter, but it's a different debate, and the applause line in sentence 5 hides the swap.

prompt_instruction: Click the faulty analogy the argument depends on.

passage_segments.text: We've always run this department like a family.
And you don't fire family members when times are hard.
So there should be no redundancies this year.
Revenue fell by 30% last year.

options.text: Family membership isn't conditional on funding or contribution; employment is a contract either side can end.
options.feedback: Yes. The analogy fails on exactly the feature the conclusion needs.
True, but not the difference that matters for redundancies.
Doesn't address why the comparison fails.
Relevant data, but it doesn't explain why the analogy is flawed.

explanation_formal: The argument from analogy holds only if the compared items share the relevant property. Families and employers differ on conditionality of membership, the very property at issue.
explanation_modern: 'We're a family' sounds warm, but families don't have budgets that decide who stays. When the comparison breaks on the point that matters, so does the argument.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that carries the Bad Example the whole argument leans on.

passage_segments.text: My cousin bought an electric car, and the battery died after two years.
So electric cars are clearly unreliable.
I'd tell anyone thinking of buying one to wait ten years.
Petrol cars have had over a century to get this right.

explanation_formal: A single anecdote (s1) supports a universal judgement (s2): secundum quid, or hasty generalisation. 'Clearly' in s2 compounds it with overclaiming.
explanation_modern: One cousin, one battery, and then a verdict on every electric car. Ask how typical the example is before trusting it.

prompt_instruction: Click the conclusion that doesn't follow.

passage_segments.text: We rolled out the new onboarding emails in May.
In June, sign-ups rose by 18%.
Clearly, the emails caused the jump.
June is also when our biggest seasonal campaign runs every year.

follow_up_question.question: What would actually test the claim?

options.text: Compare with June sign-ups in previous years, or hold the emails back from a random group.
options.feedback: Yes. A baseline or a control separates the emails' effect from the seasonal campaign.

options.text: Send even more emails and see if sign-ups rise further.
options.feedback: Still confounded with everything else going on.

options.text: Ask the marketing team whether they think it worked.
options.feedback: Opinion, not evidence.
Timing is exactly what post hoc reasoning mistakes for cause.

explanation_formal: Post hoc ergo propter hoc: temporal succession is taken as causation, ignoring a known confound (s4).
explanation_modern: After is not the same as because. June always goes up, so check what the emails added on top of that.

prompt_instruction: Diagnose and respond.

passage_segments.text: If we let one team trial flexible hours, every team will want them.
Then nobody will be in the office on Fridays, and within a year we won't be able to serve clients at all.

options.feedback: Yes. A chain of unearned consequences leads to an extreme end.
Only one path is offered, but the flaw is the chain.
Not circular.
No word changes meaning.
Right: one trial ends with 'can't serve clients at all'.
'Every team will want them' is a guess, but the dominant engine is the spiral to disaster.
No feeling is offered as proof.
Close, but the shape is escalation, not a binary.

options.text: That's ridiculous. Nothing like that would happen.
options.feedback: Contradiction without a plan.

options.text: Let's run the trial with one team for three months, with a rule that Friday client cover is kept, and decide on the evidence whether to extend it.
options.feedback: Puts a guard on each feared link and makes the decision depend on data.
An unspecified Bad Example of your own.

options.text: You just don't trust your staff.
options.feedback: Mind-reading and ad hominem in one.

explanation_formal: Each link in the chain is asserted, not argued. The deliberative remedy is to bound the risk at each link with a reversible, evidence-gated trial.
explanation_modern: One trial doesn't mean no one in the office in a year. Make the trial small, reversible and measured, and the slope has nowhere to slide.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where the speaker catastrophises.

passage_segments.text: I fumbled one question in the client presentation.
Now they'll think the whole firm is incompetent, and we'll lose the account.
I should never have been put in front of them.
Next time I'll prepare a backup slide on pricing.

follow_up_question.question: Which second distortion is in the same sentence?

options.text: Mind-Reading: assuming what the client thinks
options.feedback: Yes. 'They'll think…' asserts the client's mind without evidence.
No feeling is offered as evidence in that sentence.
Not circular.
No word shifts meaning.

explanation_formal: Sentence 2 magnifies one error into total loss (catastrophising) and attributes a judgement to the client without evidence (mind-reading). Sentence 4 is the healthy deliberative turn.
explanation_modern: One fumble becomes 'we lose the account' in a single sentence. Sentence 4 is the version worth keeping: a concrete fix for next time.

register_tags.modern: I Feel It, So It's True

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that treats a feeling as evidence.

passage_segments.text: The new security policy requires two-factor login on every account.
Honestly, it makes me uneasy.
And when something feels that wrong, it usually is, so it's probably making us less safe.
Phishing-related account takeovers dropped by half in the first month.

explanation_formal: Sentence 2 reports a feeling, which is legitimate. Sentence 3 infers a fact about the world from it, which is emotional reasoning, and sentence 4 contradicts that inference.
explanation_modern: Feeling uneasy is fine. Concluding the policy makes us less safe because it feels wrong isn't, especially when the numbers point the other way.

prompt_instruction: Click the all-or-nothing judgement.

passage_segments.text: The pilot hit four of its five targets.
It missed the cost target by 3%.
So the pilot failed, and we should scrap it.
The team has already proposed a fix for the cost overrun.

explanation_formal: A graded result (four of five targets, one narrowly missed) is collapsed into a binary verdict of failure, which licenses an extreme policy.
explanation_modern: Four out of five and a 3% miss is not a failure. It's a pilot with one fixable problem.

prompt_instruction: Click the overclaim.

passage_segments.text: Our survey of 200 users found that 61% preferred the new layout.
This proves beyond doubt that all our users want the redesign.
The survey went to people who had opted in to beta features.
We'll roll it out to everyone on Monday.

options.text: Most beta users we surveyed preferred the new layout. Let's test with a representative sample before a full rollout.
options.feedback: Scoped to the sample, honest about the uncertainty, and still decisive about the next step.

options.text: Users might possibly sort of like it, maybe.
options.feedback: Over-corrected into cowardly hedging (the Coyness Index).

options.text: 61% of all users want the redesign.
options.feedback: Still generalises from a biased sample.
Throws out real information.

explanation_formal: Sentence 2 inflates a sample statistic into a universal certainty ('proves beyond doubt', 'all'). Sentence 3 shows the sample isn't representative.
explanation_modern: 61% of keen beta users is not 'all users, beyond doubt'. Say what the data shows, no more and no less.

prompt_instruction: You've received this email. Diagnose it and reply.

passage_segments.text: You didn't reply to my proposal for three days, so clearly you think it's worthless and you're hoping I'll drop it.

options.feedback: Yes. Silence gets read as a specific hostile intention.
No spiral to disaster here, just an assumed motive.
Not circular.
It's on topic, just unfounded.

options.text: I hadn't read it yet. I was on leave until Wednesday. I've read it now, and my main question is the budget in section 3.
options.feedback: Corrects the fact without accusation and moves straight to the substance.
Labels the person and heats things up.

options.text: If you're going to be like this, maybe I will.
options.feedback: Confirms their fear and escalates.
Over-apology, an all-or-nothing self-judgement, and it skips the proposal.

explanation_formal: Mind-reading attributes a specific mental state to another without evidence. The best response corrects the factual premise and redirects to the deliberative question.
explanation_modern: Three days of silence doesn't mean 'I think it's worthless'. Give the real reason, then engage with the proposal.
